title: Do penguin species differ in flipper length?
text:
Code: read the data and compute the numbers
library(tidyverse)

penguins <- read_csv("../data/example/penguins.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Mean flipper length per species (2 penguins have no measurement)
flipper_means <- penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm)) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(mean_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm))

mean_of <- function(sp) flipper_means %>% filter(species == sp) %>% pull(mean_mm)
gentoo_vs_chinstrap_mm <- mean_of("Gentoo") - mean_of("Chinstrap")
gentoo_vs_adelie_mm <- mean_of("Gentoo") - mean_of("Adelie")

n_penguins <- nrow(penguins)
n_islands <- n_distinct(penguins$island)
n_no_flipper <- sum(is.na(penguins$flipper_length_mm))
first_year <- min(penguins$year)
last_year <- max(penguins$year)




Code: make the figure
set.seed(3901)  # same jitter on every render
penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Flipper length (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Figure 1: Flipper length by species. Each point is one penguin; each box shows the middle half of a species, and the line inside it is the median.





Finding. Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers, on average about 21 mm longer than Chinstrap and 27 mm longer than Adelie penguins.
Limitation. These are 344 penguins measured on 3 islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica, in 2007–2009; 2 have no flipper measurement.
Data source. Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data (R package). https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/ License: CC0.

title: Guided Project: Statistical Transformations and Coordinate Systems
text:
Part A · Fairness
My group: Age My outcome: time_in_hospital >= 5.
Question A: “Of each age group, what share has the outcome of time_in_hospital >= 5?” Question B: “Of everyone with time_in_hospital >= 5, what share is each age group?”

A0 · My group and my outcome

a_data <- fairness %>%
  mutate(
    group = age,
    has_outcome = time_in_hospital >= 5
  )

a_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  group               has_outcome     n
  <chr>               <lgl>       <int>
1 30 years or younger FALSE         106
2 30 years or younger TRUE           35
3 30-60 years         FALSE        1012
4 30-60 years         TRUE          499
5 Over 60 years       FALSE        1962
6 Over 60 years       TRUE         1386




A1 · The rate within each group (question A)

a1 <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = NULL, fill = "Has the outcome")

show_plot(a1)







Figure 1: Share of each group with the outcome.





I would guess that older people would have a longer time in the hospital, so I expect the highest rate to be in the older age groups. The plot shows that people over 60 have the highest share of time_in_hospital >= 5, while people under 30 have the lowest share. People between 30 and 60 years sit in between. This makes groups of different sizes comparable because it brings all groups to the same scale instead of being different just because there is more people in one group or the other.


A2 · Rates with their standard error

a2_rates <- a_data %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    se = sqrt(rate * (1-rate) / n)
  )

a2 <- ggplot(a2_rates,
             aes(x = rate, y = group,
                 xmin = rate - se,
                 xmax = rate + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  # Many groups, and the labels touch the points? Keep every group, and use
  # vjust = -0.8, size = 3 instead of nudge_y = 0.3.
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Rate (share of the group with the outcome)", y = NULL)

show_plot(a2)







Figure 2: Rate in each group, with ± one standard error and the group size.





The youngest group has the widest range. It tells the reader that even though the group is small, it has a high variability in th e outcome. One or two outliers can already have a significant impact on the results.


A3 · Zoom or filter?

a3_table <- a_data %>%
  count(group) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
a3_table

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  group                   n
  <chr>               <int>
1 Over 60 years        3348
2 30-60 years          1511
3 30 years or younger   141

a3_start <- 120

a3_counts <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Count", y = NULL)

a3_zoom <- a3_counts +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)), expand = FALSE)

# A warning about removed rows here is expected (Session 2, slide 5).
a3_filter <- a3_counts +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)))

# Lie Factor (Tufte, 2001, p. 57) of the zoomed plot, largest vs smallest
# group: how many times the picture exaggerates the difference.
a3_largest <- max(a3_table$n)
a3_smallest <- min(a3_table$n)
a3_lie_factor <-
  ((a3_largest - a3_start) / (a3_smallest - a3_start)) /
  (a3_largest / a3_smallest)
a3_lie_factor

[1] 6.47363

show_plot(a3_counts)
show_plot(a3_zoom)
show_plot(a3_filter)











(a) From 0











(b) Zoomed











(c) Filtered







Figure 3: Counts per group: from 0, zoomed and filtered.




The zoomed plot’s Lie Factor (largest vs smallest group) is 6.5.
The first version shows the full picture with a normal scale and the whole x axis is shown from 0 up to a little more than the biggest group has. The second plot starts just slightly above the amount of the smallest group. This makes the smallest group look even less represented and is quite misleading. The third plot filters out all of the data and is therefore empty.


A4 · Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome (question B)

a4_shares <- a_data %>%
  filter(has_outcome) %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

a4 <- ggplot(a4_shares, aes(x = share, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of everyone with the outcome", y = NULL)

show_plot(a4)







Figure 4: Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome.





They do point in the same direction since the plots always confirm each other. Already in the beginning, the oldest group stood out which was then confirmed throughout.

title: Guided Project: Statistical Transformations and Coordinate Systems
text:
Part B · Sports
My group, outcome and value: group = the number of of sets played in the match, outcome = the home player won, value = the total points sccored in game 1.

  mutate(
    group = factor(Sets_P1 + Sets_P2),
    has_outcome = HomeWinner == 1,
    value = P1_G1 + P2_G1
  )

b_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)

B1 · The rate within each group

b1 <- ggplot(b_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = "Sets played", fill = "Home player won")

show_plot(b1)







Figure 5: Share of each group with the outcome.





The home player won about 50% of the matches (50.1%) in the 3-set matches, 49.5% in the 4-set matches, and 49.4% in the 5-set matches, so the link of the matches shows almost no connection to who wins. I use shares because the groups are of different sizes and it makes them comparable.


B2 · A mean with its two spreads

b2_summary <- b_data %>%
  drop_na(value) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(value),
    sd = sd(value),
    se = sd / sqrt(n)
  )

b2 <- ggplot(b2_summary,
             aes(x = mean, y = group,
                 xmin = mean - se,
                 xmax = mean + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Mean points in game 1", y = "Sets played")


show_plot(b2)







Figure 6: Mean in each group, with ± one standard error and group size.

The mean of game 1 is about 18.5 points for 3-set matches and about 18.8 points for 4- and 5-set matches, a gap of about 0.3 points. This gap is large compared to the se (each bar is only about ±0.06 points wide, and the 3-set bar does not overlap the other two), so it is unlikely to be just sampling noise. We should take from this that there is a small, fairly clear difference between the averages, not a difference that would let anyone predict the length of a match from its first game.


B3 · Zoom or filter?

b3_table <- b_data %>%
  count(group) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

b3_start <- floor(min(b3_table$n) / 2)

b3_counts <- ggplot(b_data, aes(y = group)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Count", y = "Sets played")

b3_zoom <- b3_counts +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(b3_start, max(b3_table$n)), expand = FALSE)

b3_filter <- b3_counts +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(b3_start, max(b3_table$n)))

b3_lie_factor <-
  ((max(b3_table$n) - b3_start) / (min(b3_table$n) - b3_start)) /
  (max(b3_table$n) / min(b3_table$n))

Figure 7: Counts per group: zoomed and filtered.




The Lie Factor of your zoomed plot is 1.18. The zoomed plot makes the 4 matches seem much more common than the other two even though they are pretty close. The filtered version removes the bars completely because they start at 0, which is outside of the limits.


B4 · Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome

b4_shares <- b_data %>%
  filter(has_outcome) %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

b4 <- ggplot(b4_shares, aes(x = share, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of all home wins", y = "Sets played")

show_plot(b4)







Figure 8: Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome.





B4 does not point in the same direction as B1. B1 shows almost no difference while B4 shows that 4-set matches have the largest share. This is more likely because there are more 4-set matches in total, so they make up the biggest part of the home wins just because they are the biggest group.
